t: Sanskrit, the sacred and learned language of ancient India, is first known from the hymns of the Rigveda, composed around 1500–1200 BCE and handed down by memory with great precision ever since.

Codified by the grammarian Panini around the 4th century BCE, Classical Sanskrit became the language of Hindu scripture, the great epics, philosophy, science and poetry, and of Buddhist and Jain learning, from Afghanistan to Java.

Its study in Europe from the late 18th century revealed the Indo-European family of languages, and it remains the liturgical language of Hinduism and a source of words for the languages of India and Southeast Asia.
dyk: In 1786 the British judge William Jones told the Asiatic Society in Calcutta that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were so alike that they must have sprung from a common source, “which, perhaps, no longer exists”: a founding moment of comparative linguistics.
ev: The hymns of the Rigveda are composed in the north-west of the subcontinent
A treaty of the Mitanni kingdom in Syria invokes the Indo-Aryan gods Mitra, Varuna and Indra
Panini composes the Ashtadhyayi, his grammar of Sanskrit in some four thousand rules
The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman, the first long royal inscription in Sanskrit
Aryabhata writes his treatise on astronomy and mathematics in Sanskrit verse
William Jones points out the common origin of Sanskrit, Greek and Latin
India’s constitution lists Sanskrit among the languages of the nation

f.family: Indo-European: the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-Iranian languages
f.script: For centuries transmitted orally; written from about the 1st century BCE in Brahmi and its descendants, today usually in Devanagari
f.earliest: The hymns of the Rigveda, composed around 1500–1200 BCE and preserved by memory; the first long inscription, at Junagadh, about 150 CE
f.status: The liturgical language of Hinduism and a language of scholarship; one of India’s scheduled languages, named as a mother tongue by about 25,000 people in the 2011 census
